name: tsl::htrie_map (hat-trie)
baseline: std::unordered_map<std::string, int> (memory, and speed on the Askitis set) and cedar::da double-array trie (memory and speed on the Wikipedia set)
workload: Insert then look up every key of the English Wikipedia titles dump enwiki-20170320-all-titles-in-ns0 (13,099,148 keys, average length 19.90, int value, shuffled and sorted variants) and the Dr. Askitis distinct_1 set (28,772,169 keys inserted, skew1_1 with 177,999,203 reads); memory is /proc/self/statm growth after insert, speed is ns/key.
claimed_speedup: Wikipedia, unsorted: tsl::htrie_map 402.25 MiB (peak 405.22), insert 643.10 ns/key, read 250.87 ns/key; cedar::da 1254.41 MiB, 1102.93 ns, 557.20 ns; std::unordered_map 1246.60 MiB, 590.88 ns, 173.58 ns. Derived from page data: about 3.1x less memory than both, 1.7x faster insert and 2.2x faster read than cedar::da; against std::unordered_map it is about 1.09x slower on insert and 1.45x slower on read. Askitis set: htrie_map 601.79 MiB, 485.45 ns insert, 77.80 ns read; std::unordered_map 2110.19 MiB, 554.02 ns, 105.05 ns; cedar::da 1100.05 MiB, 682.25 ns, 71.98 ns. Derived from page data: about 3.5x less memory than std::unordered_map and 1.8x less than cedar::da, with 1.14x faster insert and 1.35x faster read than std::unordered_map, but a read about 1.08x slower than cedar::da.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 6.3 on Debian Stretch x64 (libstdc++ inferred as the GCC default, not stated); gist Makefile: g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -DNDEBUG -O3 with CityHash64 as hash for the hash-table baselines; README says best of 20 runs
hardware: Intel i5-5200u laptop CPU, 8 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11 library (htrie_map and htrie_set, MIT). Any modifying operation (insert, emplace, erase) invalidates all iterators. Supports prefix search (equal_prefix_range, erase_prefix) and longest-prefix match, binary keys, serialization. Memory versus read speed is tunable with max_load_factor: README rows go from 402 MiB with read 251 ns (default) to 710 MiB with read 191 ns (max_load_factor=1) on the unsorted Wikipedia set. It is a dynamic pointer-based string dictionary, not a succinct or static structure, so the listed baselines SDSL and sux do not apply directly. Plain hash tables with reserve (tsl::hopscotch_map 119.49 ns read, tsl::array_map with reserve 128.28 ns) read faster and insert faster than it on the shuffled Wikipedia set and the Askitis set (on the sorted Wikipedia set htrie_map reads faster: 68.08 ns vs 117.20 ns for hopscotch_map with reserve).
caveats: The speed win holds against other tries (cedar::da, the C hat-trie, qp trie, crit-bit, Judy), not against hash tables: on the Wikipedia set std::unordered_map was faster (590.88 vs 643.10 ns insert, 173.58 vs 250.87 ns read), and the Askitis win over std::unordered_map is small (1.14x insert, 1.35x read) and reverses on insert if std::unordered_map is given reserve (309.06 vs 485.45 ns insert, while read stays behind at 109.89 vs 77.80 ns). The memory win over hash tables is partly caused by std::string keys costing at least 32 bytes each in those baselines (the README says so). Numbers are from 2017 hardware (laptop i5-5200u) and GCC 6.3. The gist (bench.cpp, Makefile) was read through WebFetch only, because gist.githubusercontent.com is blocked here, so flags and timing code come from the fetch tool's extraction; the README says best of 20 runs while the gist timing code looked like a single pass per invocation. Independent run, same insert and lookup protocol, found in the poplar-trie README (opened) on a Xeon E5-2680 v2 2.80 GHz, g++ 7.3.0 -O3, code at kampersanda/dictionary_bench (CMakeLists.txt opened: Release default -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=native): Wikipedia titles Sep 2018, 14,130,439 keys: tsl::htrie_map 0.43 GiB, insert 0.60 us/key, lookup 0.27 us/key; std::unordered_map 1.29 GiB, 0.50, 0.27; cedar::da reduced trie 1.19 GiB, 0.89, 0.59. UK-domain URLs, 39,459,925 keys: htrie_map 2.68 GiB, 1.08, 0.51; std::unordered_map 6.05 GiB, 0.67, 0.50; cedar::da prefix trie 2.02 GiB, 2.20, 2.28 (the cedar prefix trie uses less memory than htrie_map on this set, 2.02 vs 2.68 GiB, but its lookup is about 4.5x slower, 2.28 vs 0.51 us/key). That run confirms about 3x less memory than std::unordered_map and no speed win over it. name: NeaTS
baseline: xz (and Brotli, Zstd, Lz4, Snappy; time-series codecs Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC (sdsl dac_vector), plus LeCo and ALP per the paper)
workload: Lossless compression of 64-bit integer time series (16 datasets in the ICDE 2025 paper per search snippets): compression ratio, full decompression speed and random-access speed; the repo harness measures full decompression MB/s, random access ns per query (1e6 random indexes, 10 runs) and scan speed.
claimed_speedup: README text, no numbers on the page: NeaTS provides, simultaneously, compression ratios close to or better than the best existing compressors, a faster decompression speed, and orders of magnitude more efficient random access.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for any measurement. CMakeLists.txt sets C++23 and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS -march=native -mtune=native -mfpmath=sse -mavx512f -fno-math-errno; -O9 and -funroll-loops appear only in CMAKE_C_FLAGS; no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE default is set
stars_or_usage: 13 stars; ICDE 2025 paper (Guerra, Vinciguerra, Boffa, Ferragina), pages 1579-1592
tradeoffs: Research code, GPL-3.0 (README says released for academic purposes under GPL-3.0) with sdsl-lite and sux vendored in lib/. Needs a C++23 compiler (GCC 13 or Clang 16 or newer), CMake 3.22, and Squash 0.7 for the Benchmark target. SIMD decompression uses std::experimental::simd and the build adds -mavx512f and -march=native, so binaries are not portable. Input is binary 64-bit signed integers with a user-chosen maximum residual bit width, so floating-point series must be converted to integers first. Compression (piecewise nonlinear model partitioning) is the expensive side; random access works on the compressed form without full decompression, which block-based general compressors cannot do.
caveats: Paper numbers could not be read: arXiv, IEEE and the author's talk slides are blocked here, and no PDF or result table is checked into the repo (root has LeaTS.cpp, NeaTSL.cpp, SNeaTS.cpp, main_simd.cpp, CMakeLists.txt; benchmark/ holds Chimp, Chimp128, Gorilla, TSXor sources, neats_lossless.cpp, gp_compressors_bench.hpp, st_compressors_bench.hpp; the datasets are on a d4science link not opened). What the search snippets said, not verified on any opened page: NeaTS reaches compression ratios close to xz and Brotli with up to 1 order of magnitude faster decompression and 3 orders of magnitude faster random access (talk-slide snippet); fastest decompression on 10 of 16 datasets; ratio better than Zstd by 28.49% on average, better than Lz4 by 52.77% and Snappy by 50.20%; faster compression than LeCo by 36.26% and ratio better by 12.80% on average; compared compressors Xz, Brotli, Zstd, Lz4, Snappy, Chimp, Chimp128, TSXor, DAC, Gorilla, LeCo, ALP. A snippet figure of 2561.31 MB/s decompression for NeaTS next to PLA 2997.00 and AA 2420.20 appears to belong to the lossy NeaTS-L comparison against PLA and AA, so it is not used as the lossless claim. Repo evidence is thin: benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp main() currently runs only squash_scan with lz4 and has everything else commented out; main_simd.cpp prints NeaTS compression, random-access and full decompression speed but its final 'Decompression speed' line times a SIMD copy of the raw data, not NeaTS; LeCo and ALP are not in the repo harness; no CPU model or build flags are given. The README's plain 'cmake ..' sets no optimization level for C++ code (only the C flags have -O9), so a default build is unoptimized unless -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release is passed. Tier C is a placeholder: the paper is peer reviewed (B), and A is possible if it states CPU, compiler and flags since the comparator harness is public; retier when arXiv 2412.16266 or the IEEE page is readable. Files opened: raw README.md, CMakeLists.txt, main_simd.cpp and benchmark/neats_lossless.cpp of and-gue/NeaTS; github.com/and-gue/NeaTS, /commits, /tree/main/benchmark, /tree/main/lib, /tree/main/include.
